doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Staying in touch with Carter: People Time and The Meaning of the Blues
summary: Carter's help with a lead sheet for Bobby Troup's tune leads to talk of Miles's reworking of melodies.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Do you still keep up with each other?

We talk once in a while. I called him recently to tell him that we were going to record one of his little-known compositions, a lovely ballad called People Time, with [Robert] Farnon, on the Farnon thing that's coming up soon. [This was released on the CD Tangence.] He was very pleased. I told Benny that I was having trouble getting a bona fide lead sheet on The Meaning of the Blues. He said, "Oh! Bobby Troup. I’m going to see Bobby Troup in a few days. I’ll tell him that you're looking for that, and I’ll get a lead sheet for you." I had been looking for weeks to get an authentic, original lead sheet of The Meaning of the Blues. We had Miles’s version, of course. What’s interesting is that when you finally get a lead sheet . . .
How different it looks.
Oh, it's got nothing to do with what Miles played. Miles created an original melody of his own on Bobby Troup’s tune.
[Michael] Brecker did that, too, on [the recording] Don't Try This . . . I can’t remember which album it's on that he does The Meaning of the Blues. [It's on Now You See It . . . (Now You Don't).]
Oh, really? I didn’t know that.
It's very beautiful.
I didn’t know that.
But I’m sure it's very different than what Bobby had in mind.
Miles's interpretation – it's a classic. It's a classic.
Like what Miles did with [Baker sings When Lights are Low].
Oh, yeah. Yeah. That’s Benny’s tune.
And Miles played the same thing up a fourth as the bridge.
That’s right, and that’s not the bridge.
No, I know.
No. Benny wrote a wonderful bridge, but Miles ignored it. [laughs]
[sings Benny Carter's bridge]
Miles went his own way on the bridge.
I that says something about you, the fact that you go back and try to find what the composer had [in mind]. That's because you’re a composer, too.
Yeah.
Go back and find out what the composer has in mind when you get ready to record a piece.
Yeah. Yeah, that’s true.
